properties.areaDesc: Bryan, GA; Chatham, GA
properties.headline: Flood Advisory issued October 10 at 7:48AM EDT until October 10 at 9:15AM EDT by NWS Charleston SC
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues.

* WHERE...Bryan County in southeastern Georgia...
Chatham County in southeastern Georgia...

* WHEN...Until 915 AM EDT.

* IMPACTS...Minor flooding in low-lying and poor drainage areas.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 747 AM EDT, Doppler radar indicated heavy rain. Minor flooding
is ongoing or expected to begin shortly in the advisory area.
- The earlier area of heavy rainfall has since lifted north of
Chatham County. Additional showers will pass through over the
next 60 to 90 minutes and could produce brief periods of light to
moderate rain.
- Some locations that will experience flooding include...
Tybee Island, Midtown Savannah, Coffee Bluff, Windsor Forest,
Hunter Army Airfield, Wilmington Island, Downtown Savannah,
Hutchinson Island, Fort Pulaski National Monument and Montgomery.
properties.instruction:
Turn around, don't drown when encountering flooded roads. Most flood
deaths occur in vehicles.

Report flooding directly to the Charleston National Weather Service
at 1-888-383-2024 or email your reports to nws.charlestonsc@noaa.gov.

NWSheadline: FLOOD ADVISORY REMAINS IN EFFECT UNTIL 915 AM EDT THIS MORNING

properties.areaDesc: Upper Hood River Valley
properties.headline: Frost Advisory issued October 10 at 4:30AM PDT until October 11 at 9:00AM PDT by NWS Portland OR
properties.description:
* WHAT...Temperatures as low as 33 to 36 degrees will result in frost
formation.

* WHERE...Upper Hood River Valley County, especially near Parkdale.

* WHEN...From midnight tonight to 9 AM PDT Sunday.

* IMPACTS...Frost could harm sensitive outdoor vegetation. Sensitive
outdoor plants may be killed if left uncovered.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...Chances for sub-freezing temperatures below 32
degrees are high in Parkdale and Dee (70-90%) tonight into Sunday
morning. However, the majority of the Upper Hood River Valley
should remain above freezing with lows of 33 to 36 degrees,
including in Odell.
properties.instruction:
Take steps now to protect tender outdoor plants from the cold.
Consider temporarily moving outdoor potted plants indoors if they are
sensitive to cold temperatures.

Consider temporarily covering sensitive plants with a lightweight
cotton fabric (i.e., bedsheets, thin blankets), as this will help
retain heat and provide frost protection for your plants.

NWSheadline: FROST ADVISORY REMAINS IN EFFECT FROM MIDNIGHT TONIGHT TO 9 AM PDT SUNDAY

properties.areaDesc: Charleston, SC
properties.headline: Flash Flood Warning issued October 10 at 7:23AM EDT until October 10 at 9:30AM EDT by NWS Charleston SC
properties.description:
At 723 AM EDT, City of Charleston Emergency Management reported heavy
rain in Downtown Charleston. Flash flooding is already occurring with
several road closures across the city.

HAZARD...Flash flooding caused by thunderstorms.

SOURCE...City of Charleston Emergency Management reported.

IMPACT...Flash flooding of small creeks and streams, urban areas,
highways, streets and underpasses as well as other poor
drainage and low-lying areas.

Some locations that will experience flash flooding include...
North Charleston, Mount Pleasant, James Island, Johns Island, West
Ashley, Downtown Charleston, Fort Sumter, Daniel Island, Folly
Beach and Kiawah Island.

An area of intense rainfall moved through the Folly Beach, James
Island, Johns Island, West Ashley, and Downtown Charleston areas and
produced 1 to 2 inches of rain. The heaviest rain has now lifted
northward but light to occasionally moderate rain will continue.
Additional rounds of heavy rain could develop through mid morning.
City of Charleston Emergency Management reported several roads closed
across the Downtown Charleston area and flash flooding is ongoing.
Additionally, a inundation depth sensor on Ogier Street near Calhoun
Street reported an inundation depth of over half of a foot.
properties.instruction:
Turn around, don't drown when encountering flooded roads. Most flood
deaths occur in vehicles.

Report flooding directly to the Charleston National Weather Service
at 1-888-383-2024 or email your reports to nws.charlestonsc@noaa.gov.

properties.headline: Special Weather Statement issued October 10 at 6:20AM EDT by NWS Jackson KY
properties.description:
A period of strong wind gusts is expected today as the remnants
of Hurricane Isaias move into eastern Kentucky. Southeasterly
winds of 10 to 20 mph, with gusts up to 35 mph are expected. The
strongest winds are expected during the afternoon and should
coincide with the arrival of the leading bands of rain. Once
rainfall becomes steady, many areas will see the winds lighten,
except at elevations above 1,500 feet, where the gusty winds are
expected to continue into the night. Isolated gusts over 40 mph
are possible over the highest ridge tops. The gusty winds could
blow around unsecured outdoor objects and decor.

properties.areaDesc: Southeastern Elko County; Ruby Mountains and East Humboldt Range; White Pine County; South Central Elko County; Northwestern Nye County; Northeastern Nye County
properties.headline: Flood Watch issued October 10 at 3:17AM PDT until October 12 at 5:00AM PDT by NWS Elko NV
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall and debris flows
are possible.

* WHERE...Portions of eastern, northeast, and south central Nevada,
including the following areas, in eastern Nevada, White Pine. In
northeast Nevada, the Ruby Mountains and East Humboldt Range in
Elko, South Central Elko and Southeastern Elko. In south central
Nevada, Northeastern Nye and Northwestern Nye.

* WHEN...From this evening through late Sunday night.

* IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers,
creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations. In
addition, flash flooding is possible over recently burned areas
like the former Ward Fire, Kearny Fire, Oxley Fire, Secret Pass
Fire, Star Valley Fire, Jones Fire, and Egberts Fire. Other burn
scar locations in the watch area could also be affected.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- Deep moisture from decaying Hurricane Rachel is expected to move
northward, crossing into portions of east-central and eastern
Nevada late tonight through roughly Monday. This significant
moisture will interact with upper level low pressure to bring
widespread showers with isolated thunderstorms to the watch area.
Moderate to locally heavy rain will cause excessive runoff and
may result in rock, mud, and debris flows in and near former fire
burned areas, steep terrain, and poorly drained urban areas.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
You should monitor later forecasts and be prepared to take action
should Flash Flood Warnings be issued.

forecast.

at 4:15 AM CDT Saturday was 16.9 feet.

this afternoon. It will then fall below flood stage tomorrow
morning.

feet on 04/13/1978.

properties.areaDesc: San Diego County Coastal Areas; San Diego County Inland Valleys; San Diego County Mountains; San Diego County Deserts
properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 10 at 2:40AM PDT by NWS San Diego CA
properties.description:
HLSSGX

This product covers EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA

**Tropical Storm Rachel Will Bring Coastal Flooding, Wind, and Rain
to Portions of Southern California Sunday**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for San Diego County
Coastal Areas, San Diego County Deserts, San Diego County
Mountains, and San Diego County Valleys

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 670 miles south-southwest of San Mateo Point CA or about
630 miles south-southwest of Mouth of Tijuana River CA
- 24.2N 121.4W
- Storm Intensity 60 mph
- Movement Northeast or 50 degrees at 22 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Tropical Storm Rachel is currently about 600 miles southwest of San
Diego, moving northeast towards Northern Baja at about 19 kts. Rachel
is expected to make landfall somewhere just south of the US/Mexico
Border Saturday evening. Tropical storm level impacts will likely
affect San Diego County. A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for all of
San Diego County. The main concerns with Tropical Storm Rachel are
coastal flooding, wind, and periods of heavy rain which could lead to
localized flooding and flash flooding. The majority of impacts from the
tropical storm are expected on Sunday.

South swell from Tropical Storm Rachel will arrive on Sunday. The
combination of south and northwest swells, increased onshore winds,
and high tides over 7 feet will maintain a threat of coastal flooding
and beach erosion along beaches in San Diego and Orange Counties. Surf
on Sunday is currently expected to peak at 6 to 9 feet, decreasing to
3 to 6 feet for Monday and Tuesday. Confidence in impactful coastal
flooding is high, with significant coastal flooding and beach erosion
likely.

Widespread rain is expected on Sunday from Tropical Storm Rachel.
There is expected to be a gradient in rainfall amounts with the higher
amounts on the southeastern side of the storm. Confidence is high that
the heaviest rain will occur over San Diego County mountains and
deserts. Peak rainfall rates of 0.50 to 0.60 inches are possible for
the coast and valleys, 0.50 to 0.70 inches per hour possible for the
deserts, and 0.70 to 1 inch per hour for the mountains. Current
forecast has rainfall totals of 0.50 to 1.25 inches for the coast,
valleys, and deserts and 1 to 2.5 inches for the mountains. Areas of
flash and urban flooding are probable, especially where the maximum
rainfall rates occur. The San Diego River at Fashion Valley is
currently forecast to peak at 7.4 feet (just below monitor stage)
Sunday afternoon. Those with interests near the San Diego River should
continue to monitor the forecast.

Increased winds are expected with the onset and passage of Tropical
Storm Rachel. Sustained winds of 39+ mph are expected on the southeast
side of the storm. Based on the current track, more southern and
eastern parts of San Diego County are most likely to see winds of this
magnitude. Regardless, strong sustained winds and wind gusts can be
expected on Sunday. Winds will likely be enhanced by local terrain
with gusts 40 to 55 mph on the desert slopes of the mountains and into
the deserts. Local gusts up to 60 mph possible on mountain ridges and
in passes and canyons.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Prepare for hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA. Potential impacts in this area
include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted, especially in coastal and valley locations that
don't typically experience strong winds. Some fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA, little to no impact
is anticipated.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across San Diego County. Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, arroyos, and
ditches may become dangerous rivers. In mountain areas,
destructive runoff may run quickly down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides. Flood
control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Prepare for dangerous rainfall flooding having possible significant
impacts across San Diego County.

* OTHER COASTAL HAZARDS:
High tides over 7 ft, combined with high surf and gusty onshore winds
will increase the threat for coastal flooding across area beaches.
Additionally surf of 6 to 9 ft will create dangerous swimming
conditions. There is increasing potential for significant coastal
flooding and beach erosion.

* TORNADOES:
Little to no impacts are anticipated at this time across EXTREME
SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to check your emergency plan and emergency supplies
kit and take necessary actions to protect your family and secure your
home or business.

When making safety and preparedness decisions, do not focus on the
exact forecast track since hazards such as flooding rain, damaging
wind gusts, storm surge, and tornadoes extend well away from the
center of the storm.

If in a place that is vulnerable to high wind, such as near large
trees, a manufactured home, upper floors of a high-rise building, or
on a boat, plan to move to safe shelter.

If you live in a place particularly vulnerable to flooding, such as
near the ocean or a large inland lake, in a low-lying or poor
drainage area, in a valley, or near an already swollen river, plan to
move to safe shelter on higher ground.

Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with orders that
are issued. Do not needlessly jeopardize your life or the lives of
others.

When securing your property, outside preparations should be concluded
as soon as possible before conditions deteriorate. The onset of
strong gusty winds or flooding can cause certain preparedness
activities to become unsafe.

Be sure to let friends and family members know of your intentions for
weathering the storm and your whereabouts. Have someone located away
from the threatened area serve as your point of contact. Share vital
contact information with others. Keep cell phones handy and charged.

Check on those who may not be fully aware of the situation or who are
unable to make personal preparations.

If you are a visitor, know the name of the county or parish in which
you are located and where it is relative to current watches and
warnings. If staying at a hotel, ask the management staff about their
onsite disaster plan. Listen for evacuation orders, especially
pertaining to area visitors.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio and local news
outlets for official storm information. Listen for possible changes
to the forecast.

There is a threat from tornadoes with this storm. Have multiple ways
to receive Tornado Warnings. Be ready to shelter quickly.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in San Diego CA around 8 AM PDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 10 at 5:23AM EDT by NWS Peachtree City GA
properties.description:
HLSFFC

This product covers North and Central Georgia

**ISAIAS MOVING INLAND OVER ALABAMA**
**FLASH FLOODING AND TORNADO RISKS CONTINUE INTO TONIGHT**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- The Tropical Storm Warning has been cancelled for
Chattahoochee, Harris, Heard, Macon, Marion, Meriwether,
Muscogee, Pike, Schley, Stewart, Sumter, Talbot, Taylor, Troup,
Upson, and Webster

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 170 miles southwest of Atlanta GA or about 90 miles
west-southwest of Columbus GA
- 32.0N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 35 mph
- Movement North or 360 degrees at 14 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

As of 5 AM EDT, Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias was moving northward
across Alabama at 14 MPH with maximum sustained winds of 35 MPH.
Widespread and potentially significant impacts are starting to unfold
across North and Central Georgia on the eastern side of Isaias. These
include a prolonged period of strong winds, heavy rainfall with
localized flooding, and the potential for several tornadoes. Impacts
will peak in intensity today into tonight as Isaias continues moving
north across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley.

While Isaias is weakening and has become post-tropical, there will be
a very strong pressure gradient between the system and strong high
pressure over the Mid-Atlantic. This gradient will support a prolonged
period of strong easterly winds with frequent gusts to 40 to 50 mph
across most of North Georgia through this afternoon and into tonight.
A High Wind Warning is in effect for this area. Areas to the south of
these warnings are in a Wind Advisory where winds will be weaker,
though gusts up to 40 mph will be possible. Across all areas, the
prolonged and strong winds could lead to power outages from downed
limbs and trees, especially when combined with saturated soils from
periods of heavy rain.

Isaias will continue to bring widespread rainfall to the area, with
multiple bands of heavy rain expected through early Sunday. Widespread
rainfall totals of 2 to 4 inches are likely across much of the area. A
localized swath of as much as 8 inches will be possible where the
heaviest banding sets up. This rainfall could lead to flash flooding,
particularly in urban and poor-drainge areas, as well as flood-prone
creeks and streams. The north-south orientation of bands may enhance
river flooding along north-south reaches. Training heavy rain in the
mountains may furthermore increase the risk of landslides. A Flood
Watch remains in effect for the entire area, as a result.

Additionally, a favorable environment for tornadoes is starting to
develop across Central Georgia early this morning, and will advance
into north Georgia by the afternoon and evening. Several tornadoes will
be possible, particularly within the outer rainbands of the system.
Tornadoes from tropical systems are typically quick to develop and
short-lived, but with the forward speed of the system and the unique
setup, we can't rule out a stronger (EF2 or EF3), long-track tornado,
especially across Central Georgia.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Potential impacts from the main wind event are now unfolding across
North and Central Georgia. Remain well sheltered from hazardous wind
having potentially significant impacts. If realized, these impacts
include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted. Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Potential impacts from the flooding rain are still unfolding across
North and Central Georgia. Remain well guarded against life-
threatening flood waters having possible extensive impacts. If
realized, these impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, arroyos, and
ditches may become dangerous rivers. In mountain areas,
destructive runoff may run quickly down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides. Flood
control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous. Many
road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

* TORNADOES:
Potential impacts from tornadoes are still unfolding across North and
Central Georgia. Remain well braced against a dangerous tornado event
having possible significant impacts. If realized, these impacts
include:
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few spots
of considerable damage, power loss, and communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile
homes demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped or
uprooted, vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed about.
Dangerous projectiles can add to the toll.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to stay inside and away from windows. Listen for
updates and be ready in case you lose electrical power. Keep a battery-
powered radio, charged cell phone and flashlight handy.

During the peak of the storm be ready to move quickly. Keep your
shoes on and rain gear handy. Boots and athletic shoes offer the best
foot protection if you become unexpectedly exposed to the weather.

Keep your cell phone charged and in power-saving mode. If you lose
power, use it sparingly and mainly for personal emergencies and
check-ins.

If you are prone to flooding or in an area under a storm surge watch
or warning, be prepared for the possibility of a quick and dramatic
rise in water levels.

If a tornado warning is issued for your area, quickly move to the
safest place within your shelter. Protect your head and body.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on creating an emergency plan see ready.ga.gov
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

As it pertains to this event...this will be the last local statement
issued by the National Weather Service in Peachtree City GA regarding
the effects of tropical cyclone hazards upon the area.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 10 at 5:09AM EDT by NWS Tallahassee FL
properties.description:
HLSTAE

This product covers eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend, southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia

**POST-TROPICAL CYCLONE ISAIAS CONTINUES PULLING AWAY FROM THE
REGION. ALL TROPICAL HEADLINES HAVE BEEN DROPPED**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- All watches and warnings have been canceled

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 140 miles north-northwest of Panama City or about 180
miles north-northwest of Apalachicola
- 32.0N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 35 mph
- Movement North or 360 degrees at 14 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

At 5 AM ET, Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias was moving north at 20 mph
over Southern Alabama with max sustained winds of 35 mph. This
downgraded system has pulled far enough away from the region to warrant
dropping all tropical headlines with this advisory cycle.

The previous Storm Surge Warning has been replaced by a Coastal Flood
Advisory for the FL Panhandle and Big Bend Forgotten coast where
inundation values of 1 to 3 feet above normally dry ground are possible
through today.

Very heavy rain was observed earlier this evening mainly along and
just east of Isaias' track. Radar-estimated amounts highlight a swath
of 7 to 8 inches from coastal Walton County, FL into western Geneva,
and Coffee County, AL with isolated amounts in excess of 10 inches.
Standing water is likely at those locations. Although much of the
flooding rain threat has subsided, additional bands of showers with
embedded heavy rain are expected to focus across the Forgotten Coast,
Florida Big Bend, and I-75 corridor. A Flood Watch remains in effect
for points east of US-19.

The tornado risk has also diminished substantially overnight, but
there is another window of opportunity for potential tornadic
circulations within the aforementioned bands through this afternoon.

Despite the overall improved weather conditions, residents are urged
to remain vigilant with respect to damage in the form of downed trees
and power lines, in addition to any standing water from flooding rains,
and continued hazardous beach conditions.Listen to local officials
during any cleanup efforts. Exercise caution if affected by power
outages.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Additional impacts from flooding rain are still a concern across the
Florida Big Bend and parts of Southwest Georgia. Remain well guarded
against dangerous flood waters having further impacts of significant
potential.

* TORNADOES:
Additional impacts from tornadoes are still a concern across the
Florida Big Bend and parts of Southwest Georgia. Remain well braced
against dangerous tornado event having further significant impact
potential.

* SURGE:
Minor impacts are anticipated at this time across eastern Florida
Panhandle and Big Bend Forgotten Coast.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:

Check in with your emergency points of contact. Let them know your
location and status. Keep conversations short and to the point. Do
not tie up communications systems.

Check on your neighbors. If necessary, help them connect with their
points of contact.

Do not attempt to return to evacuated areas until local authorities
have inspected roads and bridges and have given the all clear.
Hazards like downed power lines and trees, washed out roads,
continued flooding in low lying areas and non-functioning traffic
lights make travel difficult.

Do not go sightseeing within impacted communities. Sightseers
interfere with the emergency work of first responders.

When inspecting damage, use flashlights rather than candles or flamed
lanterns. Be aware of sparks that can ignite natural gas or other
leaking flammables.

When clearing out fallen trees, be careful with chainsaws and axes.
Always wear protective gear and keep others at a safe distance.
Leaning trees and those which have fallen on roofs or power lines can
be especially dangerous. If you are not in good health or unsure
about what you are doing, have someone with tree cutting experience
do the job. Never cut trees without a partner.

If using a generator, avoid carbon monoxide poisoning by following
instructions provided by the manufacturer. Operate your generator in
a well-ventilated space outside of your living area and away from
open doors and windows.

Problems with sewer backups can further contaminate standing flood
waters. Keep children away from flood waters. Also, listen for boil
water alerts as tap water may have become non-potable.

Be alert for potential flooding from rising rivers and streams which
may have yet to crest. Remain informed of the latest river forecasts
and heed any flood watches and warnings.

Be alert for flooded roads which could be compromised or littered
with debris. Avoid travel until water levels subside and roads have
been cleared. Do not drive through places where flood waters cover
the road. Turn around, don't drown!

Have multiple ways to receive Tornado Warnings if issued. Consider
nearby shelter options as you move about. Be ready to shelter quickly.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

As it pertains to this event...this will be the last local statement
issued by the National Weather Service in Tallahassee FL regarding
the effects of tropical cyclone hazards upon the area.

properties.description:
HLSBMX

This product covers Central Alabama

** Flash flooding risk continues across all of Central Alabama **

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- All watches and warnings have been canceled

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 110 miles south of Birmingham AL or about 30 miles
south-southwest of Montgomery AL
- 32.0N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 35 mph
- Movement North or 360 degrees at 14 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Hurricane Isaias made landfall earlier this evening near Destin, FL
with max sustained winds of 105 MPH and a central pressure of 971 mb.
The system has since become quite disorganized with the center becoming
ill defined and has become post-tropical with the characteristic
broadening wind field and expanding precipitation area. Further
weakening is expected as the system continues to move north then
northeast into Eastern Tennessee and toward the Mid Atlantic States.
With the system now post-tropical, we are discontinuing all tropical-
based products. The Tropical Storm Warning is being replaced by a Wind
Advisory and the High Wind Warning will remain in effect across our far
northeast counties.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Little to no additional wind impacts expected.
- Community officials are now assessing the extent of actual wind
impacts accordingly.
- Emergency work crews are restoring essential community
infrastructure as necessary.
- If you have an emergency dial 9 1 1.


Elsewhere across Central Alabama, little to no impact is anticipated.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Additional impacts from flooding rain are still a concern across
Central Alabama. Remain well guarded against locally hazardous flood
waters having further impacts of limited potential.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Remain safely sheltered until conditions improve. When going outside
be sure to stay away from downed power lines, hazardous debris and
flooded areas.

If your home or shelter was damaged, be alert to the smell of gas
leaks and be cautious around electrical wiring, broken glass, jagged
metal and wood, and protruding nails and screws.

Check to see if everyone in your group is OK. Administer first aid to
those who are injured. If possible, call 9 1 1 for any serious
injuries. Remember, it may be difficult for emergency responders to
arrive quickly.

Check in with your emergency points of contact. Let them know your
location and status. Keep conversations short and to the point. Do
not tie up communications systems.

Check on your neighbors. If necessary, help them connect with their
points of contact.

Allow extra time for emergency vehicles to reach you as they navigate
road hazards.

When entering areas that have been heavily damaged, bring along a
GPS-enabled device to help with street navigation. Do not drive on
roads that have been marked closed.

Do not go sightseeing within impacted communities. Sightseers
interfere with the emergency work of first responders.

When inspecting damage, use flashlights rather than candles or flamed
lanterns. Be aware of sparks that can ignite natural gas or other
leaking flammables.

Do not go up on your roof until the weather conditions are safe.
Ladders can be slippery in the rain and unexpected wind gusts can
blow you off the roof.

When clearing out fallen trees, be careful with chainsaws and axes.
Always wear protective gear and keep others at a safe distance.
Leaning trees and those which have fallen on roofs or power lines can
be especially dangerous. If you are not in good health or unsure
about what you are doing, have someone with tree cutting experience
do the job. Never cut trees without a partner.

If using a generator, avoid carbon monoxide poisoning by following
instructions provided by the manufacturer. Operate your generator in
a well-ventilated space outside of your living area and away from
open doors and windows.

Problems with sewer backups can further contaminate standing flood
waters. Keep children away from flood waters. Also, listen for boil
water alerts as tap water may have become non-potable.

Be alert for any lingering wind gusts which could take down weakened
trees and/or power lines, collapse damaged structures, or cause
flying debris.

Be alert for potential flooding from rising rivers and streams which
may have yet to crest. Remain informed of the latest river forecasts
and heed any flood watches and warnings.

Be alert for flooded roads which could be compromised or littered
with debris. Avoid travel until water levels subside and roads have
been cleared. Do not drive through places where flood waters cover
the road. Turn around, don't drown!

Have multiple ways to receive Tornado Warnings if issued. Consider
nearby shelter options as you move about. Be ready to shelter quickly.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

As it pertains to this event...this will be the last local statement
issued by the National Weather Service in Birmingham AL regarding the
effects of tropical cyclone hazards upon the area.

properties.areaDesc: South Walton; Coastal Bay
properties.headline: High Surf Warning issued October 10 at 4:52AM EDT until October 11 at 11:00AM EDT by NWS Tallahassee FL
properties.description:
* WHAT...For the Coastal Flood Advisory, minor coastal flooding.
For the High Surf Warning, dangerously large breaking waves of
2 to 14 feet in the surf zone. For the High Rip Current Risk,
dangerous rip currents.

* WHERE...South Walton and Coastal Bay Counties.

* WHEN...For the Coastal Flood Advisory, until 11 AM CDT this
morning. For the High Surf Warning, until 10 AM CDT Sunday.
For the High Rip Current Risk, through late Sunday night.

* IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only
isolated road closures expected. Breaking waves can sweep
people off jetties and docks, and into dangerous seas. Life-
threatening swimming conditions and significant beach erosion
can be expected. Rip currents can sweep even the best swimmers
away from shore into deeper water.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...Minor to locally moderate coastal flooding
will continue through today.
properties.instruction:
If travel is required, allow extra time as some roads may be
closed. Do not drive around barricades or through water of
unknown depth. Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone
property.

Everyone should remain out of the water due to life-threatening
surf conditions. Stay off of jetties, piers, and other waterside
infrastructure.

Swim near a lifeguard. If caught in a rip current, relax and
float. Don't swim against the current. If able, swim in a
direction following the shoreline. If unable to escape, face the
shore and call or wave for help.

properties.description:

by mid to late morning. Wind speeds will ease across east-central
South Dakota by mid afternoon, while the stronger gusts linger in
southwest Minnesota through sunset.

levels as low as 25 to 35 percent, will produce elevated fire
weather concerns today. Grassland fire danger will reach the High
category, with locally higher fire danger in cured croplands and
grasses.

crops, as rapid fire spread is possible.

may produce areas of blowing dust, locally reducing visibility and
air quality.

float. Don't swim against the current. If able, swim in a
direction following the shoreline. If unable to escape, face the
shore and call or wave for help.

properties.headline: Flood Warning issued October 10 at 3:35AM EDT until October 10 at 12:45PM EDT by NWS Tallahassee FL
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall is expected.

* WHERE...Coffee County in southeastern Alabama...
Western Dale County in southeastern Alabama...
Geneva County in southeastern Alabama...

* WHEN...Until 1145 AM CDT Saturday.

* IMPACTS...Flooding of rivers, creeks, streams, and other low-lying
and flood-prone locations is imminent or occurring. Numerous roads
remain closed due to flooding. Streams continue to rise due to
excess runoff from earlier rainfall. It will take several hours for
all the water from these storms to work through local drainage
systems in urban areas.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 232 AM CDT, Extremely heavy rain on Friday night due to
Hurricane Isaias brought 5 to 12 inches of rain to the warned
area. Heavy rain has ended, but small streams, creeks and rivers
will continue to rise and flood for at least several more hours
as water moves downhill and downstream.
- Flooding impacts will continue, but no additional rainfall is
expected.
- Some locations that will experience flooding include...
Daleville, Elba, Enterprise, Fort Rucker, Geneva, Ozark, Level
Plains, Samson, New Brockton, Ariton, Lee, Clayhatchee, Kinston,
Coffee Springs, Enterprise Municipal A/P, Turner Crossroads,
Battens Crossroads, Lucile and Shell Army Field.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
Turn around, don't drown when encountering flooded roads. Most flood
deaths occur in vehicles.

Be aware of your surroundings and do not drive on flooded roads.

In hilly terrain there are hundreds of low water crossings which are
potentially dangerous in heavy rain. Do not attempt to cross flooded
roads. Find an alternate route.

------------------

properties.description:
HLSMEG

This product covers Mid-South

**THE REMNANTS OF ISAIAS WILL CONTINUE TO MOVE NORTH OVERNIGHT**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- All watches and warnings have been canceled

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 320 miles southeast of Memphis TN or about 230 miles
southeast of Tupelo MS
- 31.5N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 65 mph
- Movement North or 355 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Hurricane Isaias made landfall around 8:30 PM CDT this evening near
Destin, FL and quickly became post-tropical. Its remnants will move
inland through Saturday, bringing gusty winds and heavy rainfall across
portions of the Mid-South. A wind advisory will replace the Tropical
Storm Warning and a flooding threat continues.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
northeast Mississippi. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted. Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across Mid-South, little to no impact is anticipated.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible significant
impacts across northeast Mississippi. Potential impacts include:
- Moderate rainfall flooding may prompt several evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may quickly become swollen with swifter
currents and overspill their banks in a few places, especially
in usually vulnerable spots. Small streams, creeks, canals,
arroyos, and ditches overflow.
- Flood waters can enter some structures or weaken foundations.
Several places may experience expanded areas of rapid
inundation at underpasses, low-lying spots, and poor drainage
areas. Some streets and parking lots take on moving water as
storm drains and retention ponds overflow. Driving conditions
become hazardous. Some road and bridge closures.

Protect against locally hazardous rainfall flooding having possible
limited impacts across northeast Mississippi.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Memphis TN as conditions warrant.

properties.headline: Hydrologic Outlook issued October 9 at 8:00PM SST by NWS Pago Pago  AS
properties.description:
ESFPPG

An active trough to the north is projected to drift southward and
move over the territory by around Tuesday of next week. This
trough is likely to remain strong and active through the duration
of next week, and may even intensify with embedded low pressure
centers. Widespread showers may be heavy and persistent at times
with the possibility of thunderstorms Tuesday through the weekend.
Widespread flash flooding may occur from this rainfall.
Landslides will be possible along steep mountainous terrain.
While there is still uncertainty in the exact magnitude and
duration of rainfall, plan now for wet conditions next Tuesday
through at least Sunday.

Keep up to date with the latest forecast information through our
internet page (www.weather.gov/ppg), local media, social media,
and our NOAA Radio broadcasts.

Sunday, south 10 to 15 mph with gusts up to 25 mph.

55-60 percent tonight. Sunday, as low as 32 percent.

* IMPACTS...Any fire that develops will catch and spread
quickly. Outdoor burning is not recommended.
properties.instruction:

are either occurring now, or will shortly. A combination of
strong winds, low relative humidity, and warm temperatures and
exceptionally dry fuels will create dangerous wildland fire
conditions. Campfires, outdoor grills, smoking materials,
fireworks, chain saws, and all-terrain vehicles all have the
potential to throw a spark and ignite a dangerous and destructive

properties.headline: Special Weather Statement issued October 10 at 1:47AM CDT by NWS Aberdeen SD
properties.description:
Warm and dry conditions will combine with strong wind gusts today
to create elevated fire weather concerns over the area this
afternoon. Due to abnormal warmth, minimum afternoon humidity
will drop to 25 to 35 percent. Strong southerly winds are expected
this morning, gusting up to 25 to 35 miles per hour. Some
localized gusts up to 45 miles per hour will be possible. Winds
are expected to decrease through the afternoon, meaning that the
strongest winds will not coincide with the lowest afternoon
humidity. However, gusts up to 30 miles per hour may linger into
the afternoon. Grassland Fire Danger will reach the High Category
as a result of the wind and humidity combination. Additionally,
these strong winds may create blowing dust today, causing
visibility reductions at times.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 10 at 2:41AM EDT by NWS Tallahassee FL
properties.description:
HLSTAE

This product covers eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend, southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia

**ISAIAS IS NOW POST-TROPICAL. MULTIPLE HAZARDS STILL REMAIN**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Warning has been issued and the Hurricane
Warning has been cancelled for Central Walton, Coastal Bay,
Coffee, Geneva, Holmes, Inland Bay, North Walton, South Walton,
and Washington

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Storm Surge Warning and Tropical Storm Warning are in effect
for Coastal Bay, Coastal Franklin, Coastal Gulf, Coastal
Jefferson, Coastal Wakulla, and South Walton
- A Storm Surge Warning is in effect for Coastal Dixie and
Coastal Taylor
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Baker, Calhoun,
Calhoun, Central Walton, Clay, Coffee, Colquitt, Dale, Decatur,
Dougherty, Early, Gadsden, Geneva, Grady, Henry, Holmes,
Houston, Inland Bay, Inland Franklin, Inland Gulf, Inland
Jefferson, Inland Wakulla, Jackson, Lee, Leon, Miller,
Mitchell, North Walton, Northern Liberty, Quitman, Randolph,
Seminole, Southern Liberty, Terrell, Thomas, Washington, and
Worth

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 110 miles north-northwest of Panama City or about 150
miles northwest of Apalachicola
- 31.5N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 65 mph
- Movement North or 355 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

At 2 AM ET, Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias was moving north at 20 mph
over Southern Alabama with max sustained winds of 65 mph. All prior
Hurricane Warnings have been replaced by Tropical Storm Warnings to
account for lingering gusty winds occasionally to around 40 mph or
higher. Other pre-existing hazards remain in effect through this
intermediate advisory cycle.

A Storm Surge Warning continues across all of our Florida Panhandle
and Big Bend coast until later this morning for inundation values of
2 to 4 feet above normally dry ground. Coastal saltwater flooding may
linger through Saturday from persistent onshore flow.

Very heavy rain was observed earlier this evening mainly along and
just east of Isaias' track. Radar-estimated amounts highlight a swath
of 7 to 8 inches from coastal Walton County, FL into western Geneva,
and Coffee County, AL with isolated amounts in excess of 10 inches.
Standing water is likely at those locations. Although much of the
flooding rain threat has subsided, additional bands of showers with
embedded heavy rain are expected to redevelop later this morning and
focus across the Forgotten Coast, Florida Big Bend, and I-75 corridor.
A Flood Watch remains in effect areawide until this evening.

The tornado risk has also diminished substantially this evening, but
there is another window of opportunity for potential tornadic
circulations within the aforementioned bands through this afternoon.

Despite the overall improved weather conditions, residents are urged
to remain vigilant with respect to damage in the form of downed trees
and power lines, in addition to any standing water from flooding
rains, and continued hazardous beach conditions.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Potential impacts from the flooding rain are still ongoing across
parts of the Tri-state area. Remain well guarded against life-
threatening flood waters having possible devastating impacts. If
realized, these impacts include:
- Extreme rainfall flooding may prompt numerous evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may overwhelmingly overflow their banks
in many places with deep moving water. Small streams, creeks, and
ditches may become raging rivers. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter numerous structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Numerous places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of raging water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become very dangerous.
Numerous road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed
out.

* SURGE:
Potential impacts from the main surge event are still ongoing across
the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend coast. Remain well away from life-
threatening surge having possible significant impacts. If realized,
these impacts include:
- Areas of inundation with storm surge flooding accentuated by
waves. Damage to several buildings, mainly near the coast.
- Sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads become
weakened or washed out, especially in usually vulnerable low
spots.
- Major beach erosion with heavy surf breaching dunes. Strong and
numerous rip currents.
- Moderate damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers.
Several small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages.

* TORNADOES:
Potential impacts from tornadoes possibly unfold across the Florida
Big Bend and parts of southwest Georgia. Remain well braced against a
dangerous tornado event having possible significant impacts. If
realized, these impacts include:
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few spots of
considerable damage, power loss, and communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile
homes demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped or
uprooted, vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed about.
Dangerous projectiles can add to the toll.

* WIND:
Potential impacts from the main wind event are ongoing across much of
the Tri-state area. Remain well sheltered from strong to gusty winds
having possible devastating impacts. If realized, these impacts
include:
- Structural damage to sturdy buildings, some with complete roof
and wall failures. Complete destruction of mobile homes. Damage
greatly accentuated by large airborne projectiles. Locations may
be uninhabitable for weeks or months.
- Numerous large trees snapped or uprooted along with fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- Many roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. Many bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Widespread power and communications outages.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:

Keep your cell phone charged and in power-saving mode. If you lose
power, use it sparingly and mainly for personal emergencies and
check-ins.

Do not be a thrill seeker or risk your life for senseless photos or
videos.

If you are prone to flooding or in an area under a storm surge watch
or warning, be prepared for the possibility of a quick and dramatic
rise in water levels.


* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Tallahassee FL around 6 AM EDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

properties.description:
* WHAT...For the Coastal Flood Advisory, up to one half foot of
inundation above ground level expected in low-lying areas near
shorelines and tidal waterways. For the High Rip Current Risk,
dangerous rip currents expected. For the High Surf Advisory,
large breaking waves of 3 to 6 feet expected in the surf zone.

* WHERE...Coastal Pender and Coastal New Hanover Counties.

* WHEN...For the Coastal Flood Advisory, from 6 AM to 10 AM EDT
this morning. For the High Rip Current Risk, from 6 AM EDT
this morning through this evening. For the High Surf Advisory,
from 2 PM this afternoon to 8 AM EDT Sunday.

* IMPACTS...Low-lying roads and locations along the Intracoastal
Waterway and adjacent tidal creeks may observe minor coastal
flooding. Check with local officials for any road closures or
impacts. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions and
localized beach erosion. Rip currents can sweep even the best
swimmers away from shore into deeper water.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...Affected areas listed are based on
average tide conditions. Additional locations may experience
flooding during periods of heavy rainfall, high winds, or
other factors.
properties.instruction:
If travel is required, allow extra time as some roads may be
closed. Do not drive around barricades or through water of
unknown depth. Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone
property.

Inexperienced swimmers should remain out of the water due to
dangerous surf conditions.

Swim near a lifeguard. If caught in a rip current, relax and
float. Don't swim against the current. If able, swim in a
direction following the shoreline. If unable to escape, face the
shore and call or wave for help.

properties.headline: Flood Watch issued October 10 at 2:32AM EDT until October 11 at 2:00PM EDT by NWS Newport/Morehead City NC
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues to be
possible.

* WHERE...A portion of eastern North Carolina, including the
following areas, Coastal Onslow, East Carteret, Hatteras Island,
Inland Onslow, Jones, Mainland Dare, Mainland Hyde, Northern Outer
Banks, Ocracoke Island, Pamlico, Southern Craven and West Carteret.

* WHEN...From 2 PM EDT this afternoon through Sunday afternoon.

* IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers,
creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations.
Flooding may occur in poor drainage and urban areas.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- A plume of tropical moisture will overspread the area and will
combine with strong lift and weak to moderate instability to
support areas of intense rainfall rates and an accompanying risk
of flooding. Total rainfall of 3 to 6 inches are forecast, with
locally higher amounts possible. The highest amounts are expected
to be where bands of thunderstorms are most persistent.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
You should monitor later forecasts and be alert for possible Flood

properties.headline: Coastal Flood Warning issued October 10 at 2:26AM EDT until October 10 at 11:00AM EDT by NWS Charleston SC
properties.description:
* WHAT...For the High Rip Current Risk, dangerous rip currents.
For the Coastal Flood Warning, one to two feet of inundation
above ground level expected along shorelines and tidal
waterways (7.9 to 8.1 feet Mean Lower Low Water at Charleston).

* WHERE...Coastal Colleton and Charleston Counties.

* WHEN...For the High Rip Current Risk, through this evening.
For the Coastal Flood Warning, from 7 AM to 11 AM EDT this
morning.

* IMPACTS...Significant saltwater inundation will render
numerous roads impassable. Properties may also flood. Rip
currents can sweep even the best swimmers away from shore into
deeper water.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...High tide will occur around 8:45 AM this
morning at Charleston. Saltwater inundation will be possible 1
to 2 hours before and after high tide.
properties.instruction:
Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. If
travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through
water of unknown depth.

Visit water.weather.gov for additional water level and flood
impact information.

Swim near a lifeguard. If caught in a rip current, relax and
float. Don't swim against the current. If able, swim in a
direction following the shoreline. If unable to escape, face the
shore and call or wave for help.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 10 at 1:22AM CDT by NWS Mobile AL
properties.description:
HLSMOB

This product covers portions of southwest Alabama...northwest Florida...south
central Alabama...and inland southeast Mississippi.

**ISAIAS MOVING OVER SOUTHERN ALABAMA**
**FLASH FLOODING AND STRONG WIND THREAT SPREADS FARTHER INLAND**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Warning has been issued and the Storm Surge
Warning and Hurricane Warning have been cancelled for Escambia
Coastal and Santa Rosa Coastal
- The Storm Surge Warning and Hurricane Warning have been
cancelled for Baldwin Central, Baldwin Coastal, Mobile Central,
and Mobile Coastal
- A Tropical Storm Warning has been issued and the Hurricane
Warning has been cancelled for Butler, Conecuh, Covington,
Crenshaw, Escambia, Escambia Inland, Monroe, Okaloosa Coastal,
Okaloosa Inland, and Santa Rosa Inland
- The Hurricane Warning has been cancelled for Baldwin Inland and
Mobile Inland
- The Tropical Storm Warning has been cancelled for Choctaw,
Clarke, George, Greene, Perry, Stone, Washington, and Wayne

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Storm Surge Warning and Tropical Storm Warning are in effect
for Okaloosa Coastal
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Butler, Conecuh,
Covington, Crenshaw, Escambia, Escambia Coastal, Escambia
Inland, Monroe, Okaloosa Inland, Santa Rosa Coastal, Santa Rosa
Inland, and Wilcox

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 110 miles east-northeast of Mobile AL or about 80 miles
north-northeast of Pensacola FL
- 31.5N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 65 mph
- Movement North or 355 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias with winds of 65 mph will continue to
move north across southern Alabama overnight. Potential damaging
wind impacts still exist east of the Alabama River, excluding Baldwin
county, with the strongest winds occurring across the northeast
portion of our warning area closest to the decaying center of
circulation. Potential impacts from these winds include downed trees
and power lines, and power outages. Storm surge will remain elevated
along the Okaloosa county coast through late tonight.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Protect against strong wind gusts having possible additional impacts
east of the Alabama river, excluding Baldwin county. Potential impacts
in this area include:
- Minor structural damage.
- Some large trees snapped or uprooted along with fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable due to debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places.
- Widespread power and communications outages.

* SURGE:
Protect against life-threatening surge having possible impacts across
coastal Okaloosa county. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Areas of inundation, mainly near the coast.
- Sections of near-shore routes and secondary roads become
weakened or washed out, especially in usually vulnerable low
spots.
- Major beach erosion with heavy surf breaching dunes. Strong and
numerous rip currents.
- Moderate damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers.
Several small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Keep cell phones well charged. Cell phone chargers for automobiles
can be helpful, but be aware of your risk for deadly carbon monoxide
poisoning if your car is left idling in a garage or other poorly
ventilated area.

It is important to remain calm, informed, and focused during an
emergency. Be patient and helpful with those you encounter.

Rising flood waters are deadly. If you are in a flood-prone
area, consider moving to higher ground. Never drive through a
flooded roadway. Remember, turn around don't drown!

If in a place that is vulnerable to high wind, such as near large
trees, a manufactured home, upper floors of a high-rise building, or
on a boat, consider moving to a safer shelter before the onset of
strong winds or flooding.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For the latest detailed evacuation and shelter information...please
refer to your local emergency management agency at the phone number
or website listed below.
- Coastal Alabama:
- Baldwin County: 251-972-6807 or
www.baldwincountyal.gov/departments/EMA
- Mobile County: 251-460-8000 or mobilecountyema.gov
- Northwest Florida:
- Escambia County: 850-471-6400 or myescambia.com/beready
- Santa Rosa County: 850-983-5360 www.santarosa.fl.gov/emergency
- Okaloosa County: 850-651-7150 or myokaloosa.com/emergency-management
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Mobile AL around 4 AM CDT, or sooner if conditions warrant.

properties.headline: Flood Watch issued October 10 at 2:06AM EDT until October 11 at 2:00PM EDT by NWS Greenville-Spartanburg SC
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues to be
possible.

* WHERE...A portion of Upstate South Carolina, including the
following areas, Abbeville, Anderson, Central Greenville, Greater
Pickens, Greenwood, Laurens, Northern Spartanburg, Southern
Greenville and Southern Spartanburg.

* WHEN...From 8 AM EDT this morning through Sunday afternoon.

* IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers,
creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations.
Creeks and streams may rise out of their banks. Low-water crossings
may be flooded.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- As Isaias weakens and moves northward through the Mid-South early
this morning, rain will become increasingly likely across the
western Carolinas and northeast Georgia. Periods of rain may
begin over the watch area before daybreak, though rainfall rates
will initially be light. Rainfall rates will increase during the
day, and heavy rain is most likely this afternoon through early
Sunday morning, particularly along the south and east facing Blue
Ridge Escarpment, that is, near the southern border of North
Carolina west of I-26, and in the sharp terrain from near Saluda
to Grandfather Mountain in North Carolina. A slow-moving band of
heavy rain may move across northeast Georgia and the Upstate of
South Carolina late this afternoon and this evening.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
A Flood Watch for flash flooding means there is a potential for rapid
onset flooding based on current forecasts. Flash flooding is a very
dangerous situation and may impact areas that do not typically flood.
Please monitor the latest forecasts and be prepared to take action
quickly should Flash Flood Warnings be issued.

and Brevard Counties.

* WHEN...Through late tonight.

* IMPACTS...Rip currents can sweep even the best swimmers away

properties.instruction:
Rip currents are powerful channels of water flowing quickly away
from shore, which occur most often at low spots or breaks in the
sandbar and in the vicinity of structures such as jetties and
piers. Heed the advice of lifeguards, beach patrol flags and
signs.

Entering the surf is strongly discouraged. If caught in a rip
current, relax and float. Don't swim against the current. If
able, swim in a direction following the shoreline. If unable to
escape, face the shore and call or wave for help.

properties.areaDesc: Buncombe, NC; Henderson, NC
properties.headline: Flood Advisory issued October 10 at 12:13AM EDT until October 12 at 2:00PM EDT by NWS Greenville-Spartanburg SC
properties.description:
...The Flood Advisory continues for the following rivers in North
Carolina...

French Broad River Near at Old Fanning Bridge Rd, 3 W Fletcher
affecting Buncombe and Henderson Counties.

.Heavy rainfall from the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will result in
excessive runoff and significant rises on streams within the upper
French Broad River watershed.  Rainfall will develop overnight
tonight, intensify during the day on Saturday, and maintain intensity
through early Sunday morning before tapering off by Sunday
mid-morning.  Storm-total rainfall of 4-8 inches is expected, with
isolated 8-10 inches possible, across the upper French Broad River
watershed, generally upstream of Etowah.  The highest totals will
occur along the Tanassee and Pisgah ridges, with lesser amounts
within the upper French Broad River valley.  Additionally, 4-6 inches
of rainfall are expected within the Mud Creek watershed in Henderson
County, which is a primary tributary of the French Broad River above
Fletcher.  While there continues to be some uncertainty regarding the
exact location, timing, and amounts of the heaviest rainfall, there
is enough confidence in the current forecast that out-of-bank
conditions are likely for the upper French Broad River.  Therefore, a
River Flood Advisory has been issued for the reach near Fletcher,
with a crest above Action Stage expected around Sunday afternoon.  A
rise above Action Stage will result in nuisance, relatively shallow
flooding of low-lying areas adjacent to the French Broad River,
including farmland, woodlands, low-lying secondary roads, greenways,
parks, and other flood-prone locations.  Additional River Flood
Advisories are possible Saturday, especially for the French Broad
River reach near Blantyre.

More significant rises along the French Broad River are possible, and
those with interests along the river are encouraged to stay weather
aware and up-to-date on the latest stream levels and forecasts at
https://water.noaa.gov/wfo/GSP.  Current reasonable worst-case
scenarios are posted in the ADDITIONAL DETAILS sections below.
Forecast crests above Minor Flood Stage may result in the River Flood
Advisories being upgraded to River Flood Warnings.

* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues.

* WHERE...French Broad River near at Old Fanning Bridge Rd, 3 W
Fletcher.

* WHEN...Until Monday afternoon.

* IMPACTS...At 10.0 feet, Action/Advisory Stage.  The French Broad
River has exceeded bankfull at the gauge site.  Isolated farmland
flooding is beginning across the French Broad River Valley from
Etowah downstream to Avery Creek upstream of the gauge site.

* At 11.5 feet, Action Stage Flooding continues.  Butler Bridge Rd.
is inundated with up to 6 inches of floodwaters from the French
Broad River, forcing road closure.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 10:30 PM EDT Friday the stage was 3.6 feet and steady.
- Forecast...The river is expected to rise to a crest of 10.6 feet
early Sunday afternoon.  A crest closer to 12 feet is possible.
A reasonable worst-case crest above Minor Flood Stage below 15
feet cannot be ruled out.
- Action/Advisory Stage is 10.0 feet.
- Minor Flood Stage is 13.0 feet.

properties.description:
...The National Weather Service in Greenville-Spartanburg has issued
a Flood Advisory for the following rivers in North Carolina...

Pigeon River above Old River Rd (NC 215), 1 SW Canton affecting
Haywood County.

.Heavy rainfall from the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will result in
excessive runoff and significant rises on streams within the upper
Pigeon River watershed.  Rainfall will develop overnight tonight,
intensify during the day on Saturday, and maintain intensity
overnight Saturday before tapering off by early Sunday morning.
Storm-total rainfall of 4-9 inches is expected, with isolated 10-11
inches possible, across the upper Pigeon River watershed, generally
upstream of Canton.  The highest totals will occur along the Pisgah
ridge and in the Shining Rock and Middle Prong Wilderness areas
within the headwaters of the east and west forks of the Pigeon River,
respectively.  While there continues to be some uncertainty regarding
the timing and amounts of the heaviest rainfall, there is enough
confidence in the current forecast that out-of-bank conditions are
likely for the Pigeon River.  Therefore, a River Flood Advisory has
been issued for the reach near Canton, with a crest above Action
Stage expected Sunday morning.  A rise above Action Stage will result
in nuisance, relatively shallow flooding of low-lying areas adjacent
to the Pigeon River, including farmland, woodlands, low-lying
secondary roads, greenways, parks, and other flood-prone locations.

More significant rises along the Pigeon River are possible, and those
with interests along the river are encouraged to stay weather aware
and up-to-date on the latest stream levels and forecasts at
https://water.noaa.gov/wfo/GSP.  Current reasonable worst-case
scenarios are posted in the ADDITIONAL DETAILS sections below.
Forecast crests above Minor Flood Stage may result in the River Flood
Advisories being upgraded to River Flood Warnings.

* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall is expected.

* WHERE...Pigeon River at above Old River Rd (NC 215), 1 SW Canton.

* WHEN...From this evening to late Sunday night.

* IMPACTS...At 8.0 feet, Action/Advisory Stage.  Common, nuisance
flooding of low-lying areas adjacent to the Pigeon River is
beginning.  Floodwaters are beginning to impact farmland,
woodlands, nurseries, parks, athletic fields, golf courses,
greenways, and boat-access areas with up to 2 feet of inundation.
Low-water crossings may be inundated with up to 2 feet of
floodwater and become impassable.  Adjacent campgrounds, mobile
home/RV parks, and secondary roads may experience floodwater
inundation of up to 1 foot.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 11:45 PM EDT Friday the stage was 1.2 feet and steady.
- Forecast...The river is expected to rise to a crest of 8.5 feet
Sunday morning.  A reasonable worst-case crest above Minor Flood
Stage below 11 feet cannot be ruled out.
- Action/Advisory Stage is 8.0 feet.
- Minor Flood Stage is 10.0 feet.

properties.description:
* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall is expected.

* WHERE...Okaloosa County in northwestern Florida...
Santa Rosa County in northwestern Florida...

* WHEN...Until 800 AM CDT Saturday.

* IMPACTS...Flooding of rivers, creeks, streams, and other low-lying
and flood-prone locations is imminent or occurring. Streams
continue to rise due to excess runoff from earlier rainfall. It
will take several hours for all the water from these storms to work
through local drainage systems in urban areas.

area due to thunderstorms. Flooding is already occurring. Between
6 and 12 inches of rain have fallen.
- Flooding impacts will continue, but no additional rainfall is
expected.
- Some locations that will experience flooding include...
Wright, Fort Walton Beach, Crestview, Niceville, Destin, Eglin
AFB, Milton, Valparaiso, Mary Esther, Bagdad, Ocean City, Lake
Lorraine, Baker, Navarre, Shalimar, Laurel Hill, Cinco Bayou,
Roeville, Point Baker and Navarre Beach.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
Turn around, don't drown when encountering flooded roads. Most flood
deaths occur in vehicles.

Be especially cautious at night when it is harder to recognize the
dangers of flooding.

Be aware of your surroundings and do not drive on flooded roads.

properties.headline: Special Weather Statement issued October 9 at 8:52PM EDT by NWS Jackson KY
properties.description:
A period of strong wind gusts is expected on Saturday as the
remnants of Hurricane Isaias move into eastern Kentucky.
Southeasterly winds of 10 to 20 mph, with gusts up to 35 mph are
expected. The strongest winds are expected during the afternoon
and should coincide with the arrival of the leading bands of rain.
Once rainfall becomes steady, many areas will see the winds
lighten, except at elevations above 1,500 feet, where the gusty
winds are expected to continue into Saturday night. Isolated gusts
over 40 mph are possible over the highest ridge tops. The gusty
winds could blow around unsecured outdoor objects and decor.

NWSheadline: Gusty Winds Expected Saturday and Saturday night with the Remnants of Hurricane Isaias

properties.areaDesc: Kenedy Island; Willacy Island; Cameron Island
properties.headline: High Surf Advisory issued October 9 at 6:34PM CDT until October 10 at 7:00PM CDT by NWS Brownsville TX
properties.description:
* WHAT...For the High Surf Advisory, large breaking waves of 4
to 7 feet in the surf zone. For the Coastal Flood Advisory,
minor coastal flooding. For the High Rip Current Risk,
dangerous rip currents.

* WHERE...Kenedy Island, Willacy Island and Cameron Island
Counties.

* WHEN...For the High Surf Advisory, until 7 PM CDT Saturday.
For the Coastal Flood Advisory, until 7 AM CDT Sunday. For the
High Rip Current Risk, through Sunday morning.

* IMPACTS...Nuisance flooding is expected, with water reaching
or pushing into the dunes on South Padre Island. Vehicles,
except those with four wheel drive and high wheel bases, will
be unable to be driven on the beach. This includes locations
north of Public Beach Access #3. Minor to moderate beach
erosion is expected. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions
and localized beach erosion. Rip currents can sweep even the
best swimmers away from shore into deeper water.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...Max inundation will occur near high tide
cycles each afternoon.
properties.instruction:
If travel is required, allow extra time as some roads may be
closed. Do not drive around barricades or through water of
unknown depth. Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone
property.

Inexperienced swimmers should remain out of the water due to
dangerous surf conditions.

Swim near a lifeguard. If caught in a rip current, relax and
float. Don't swim against the current. If able, swim in a
direction following the shoreline. If unable to escape, face the
shore and call or wave for help.

NWSheadline: COASTAL FLOOD ADVISORY REMAINS IN EFFECT UNTIL 7 AM CDT SUNDAY... ...HIGH SURF ADVISORY REMAINS IN EFFECT UNTIL 7 PM CDT SATURDAY... ...HIGH RIP CURRENT RISK REMAINS IN EFFECT THROUGH SUNDAY MORNING

properties.description:
* WHAT...For the Coastal Flood Advisory, Up to 1.4 ft of
inundation above ground level is possible in low-lying areas

Statement, increased risk of rip currents and sneaker waves
expected with breaking waves up to 16 feet.

* WHERE...San Francisco, Northern Monterey Bay and Southern
Monterey Bay and Big Sur Coast Counties.

* WHEN...For the Coastal Flood Advisory, until 3 PM PDT Tuesday.
For the Beach Hazards Statement, from Saturday morning through
Monday evening.

* IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only
isolated road closures expected. High tides will result in
flooding along coastal trails, cut off access to some low-
lying beaches and coastal areas, and bring water and waves
farther up the beach than typical. Dangerous conditions are
forecast along the shoreline. Hazards include sneaker waves,
strong rip currents, and large breaking waves.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide
is expected to be 1.4 ft above normal (7.3 ft MLLW) at 11:50 AM
Saturday 10/10, 1.4 ft above normal (7.3 ft MLLW) at 12:18 PM
Sunday 10/11, 1.2 ft above normal (7.1 ft MLLW) at 12:46 PM
Monday 10/12, and 1.1 ft above normal (7.0 ft MLLW) at 1:14 PM
Tuesday 10/13. These predictions include up to 1.2 ft of surge
that will enhance the astronomical tide and flooding threat.
High tide varies up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the
Pacific Coast and through the San Francisco Bay, respectively.
properties.instruction:

closed. Do not drive around barricades or through water of
unknown depth. Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone
property.

infrastructure. Remain out of the water to avoid hazardous surf
and NEVER turn your back on the ocean. Monitor local weather,
surf and tide forecasts at www.weather.gov/mtr.

properties.headline: Air Quality Alert issued October 9 at 4:35PM CDT by NWS Twin Cities/Chanhassen MN
properties.description:
* WHAT...The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency has issued an Air
Quality Alert for course particles pollution. The Air Quality
Index (AQI) is expected to reach the Orange or Unhealthy for
Sensitive Groups category.

* WHERE...West central and southwest Minnesota.

* WHEN...From 7 AM CDT to 7 PM CDT Saturday.

* IMPACTS...Sensitive groups, such as people with lung disease
(including asthma), heart disease, and children and older adults,
may experience health effects.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...Unseasonably warm temperatures and strong
southerly wind gusts in excess of 40 mph across dry soils in an
area of drought will result in blowing dust and reduced air
quality Saturday morning and afternoon. Decreasing winds will
lessen the potential for impacts through the evening.
properties.instruction:
Sensitive groups, such as people with lung disease (including
asthma), heart disease, and children and older adults, should
limit prolonged or heavy exertion.

Reduce or eliminate activities that contribute to air pollution,
such as outdoor burning, and use of residential wood burning
devices. Reduce vehicle trips and vehicle idling as much as
possible.
properties.note: Non-Weather Emergency Message. Not sent to IPAWS.

properties.headline: Beach Hazards Statement issued October 9 at 2:34PM PDT until October 12 at 2:00PM PDT by NWS Medford OR
properties.description:
* WHAT...A moderate risk for sneaker waves is expected. Short
period north-northwest wind waves will interact with a building
west-northwest long period swell.

* WHERE...The beaches of Douglas, Coos, and Curry counties.

* WHEN...From late Saturday night through Monday afternoon. The
risk will be highest during Sunday morning.

* IMPACTS...Sneaker waves can run up significantly farther on
beaches than normal, including over rocks and jetties. These
waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and sweep
them into the ocean. The waves can also move logs or other
objects which could crush or trap anyone caught underneath.

* View the hazard area in detail at
https://www.wrh.noaa.gov/map/?wfo=mfr
properties.instruction:

remain out of the water to avoid hazardous conditions.

properties.description:
The following statement was issued by the Oklahoma Department of
Environmental Quality from 10 AM to 10 PM CDT Saturday.

An Air Quality Alert for Ozone has been issued for Saturday, October
10th, for the Lawton area due to expected high concentrations of
ozone.

Public Health Recommendations: Persons with existing heart or
respiratory ailments should reduce physical exertion and outdoor
activity.

The general public is encouraged to help alleviate the problem by
reducing vehicle miles traveled by riding the bus, carpooling, or
avoiding unnecessary trips. The public is also asked to avoid
refueling during the morning and early afternoon hours, and to avoid
the use of two cycle engines such as lawn mowers, motorcycles, weed
trimmers, and outboard engines. It is also advised to limit outdoor
burning.

To view the latest air quality map, visit airnow.gov or the AirNow
app.

For hourly updates on concentrations and possible health warnings,
telephone the Oklahoma Department of Environmental Quality at
405-702-4100. For more information on health effects, call the
American Lung Association of Oklahoma at 405-748-4674

properties.headline: Flood Watch issued October 9 at 12:59PM MST until October 12 at 5:00AM MST by NWS Flagstaff AZ
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall is possible.

* WHERE...Yavapai, western Coconino, northern Gila, and far southern
Navajo counties.

* WHEN...From Saturday morning through late Sunday night.

* IMPACTS...Flash flooding will be possible in creeks, normally dry
washes, swimming holes, and over recently burned areas. Low-water
crossings may be flooded.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- A upper-level trough will help pull moisture from the remnants of
Tropical Storm Rachel up into western Arizona to produce showers
and thunderstorms Saturday, followed by extended periods of
rainfall through at least Sunday. Thunderstorms will have the
potential to produce heavy rainfall that could lead to flash
flooding, while extended periods of rain can lead to elevated
streams, rivers, and flow through washes. Greatest risk of heavy
rainfall looks be along higher terrain due to upsloping.
- Additional information is available at weather.gov/flagstaff.
properties.instruction:
Have a way to receive Flash Flood Warnings and be prepared to take
action should warnings be issued.
